newsitem.title: USA: Execution of Gary Gilmore echoes after 20 years.
newsitem.headline: Execution of Gary Gilmore echoes after 20 years.

text.p: Twenty years ago on Friday, a cold-blooded killer of two strangers told a firing squad at the Utah State Prison "Let's do it" and with those now-famous words ushered in an era of capital punishment in the United States that shows no signs of abating.

Since Gary Gilmore willingly, eagerly and successfully fought to become the first person executed after the Supreme Court lifted an 11-year ban on the death penalty, 359 other men and one woman have been legally put to death, often after years of appeals had been exhausted.

The state of Arkansas twice put three men to death on the same day because it was cheaper that way, and tiny Delaware last year had to locate dusty old army manuals explaining how to prepare a rope for a hanging there.

While human rights groups charge that the United States is the only industrialised nation to engage in such a barbaric practice, the death penalty has become overwelmingly popular with U.S. voters in the 20 years since Gilmore's execution.

Only 11 states have held out against it and many experts think the 1988 presidential race turned on the failure of Democrat Michael Dukakis to explain adequately why he would not want a man executed if that person had raped and murdered Dukakis' wife.

While many studies show the death penalty does not deter crime, it was not an issue in the 1996 campaign because both President Bill Clinton and Republican Bob Dole supported it. In his first term, Clinton extended the death penalty to major drug dealers, who have not overtly killed anyone, in a federal anti-crime measure that swept through Congress.

Diann Rust-Tierney, head of the American Civil Liberties Union's Capital Punishment Project, said 1997 could be a record-breaking year for executions -- surpassing 1995 when 56 people were put to death, mostly by lethal injection. Only Utah effectively allows death by firing squad and it has executed only one other convict this way since Gilmore.

Rust-Tierney and other experts said the public has become inured to executions and takes notice only when the case is controversial or the execution especially grisly or unusual, as when Arkansas put three killers to death on the same night six days ago. One man spent 45 minutes waiting on a guerney with a lethal injection needle in his arm while the Supreme Court heard and rejected his last appeal.
But the public was not bored or indifferent on Jan. 17, 1977.

The entire country waited then for word that five state highway patrolmen had poked their rifles through slits in a dark cloth screen in the cannery of the Utah State Prison and executed Gilmore, who had spent half his life in jails and had killed two Brigham Young University students he had never met before because he had a fight with his girlfriend.

"This was a man who was a cold-blooded killer who knew who he was and made no excuses. He had to make one simple decision in his life, whether or not to die, and he rose to the occasion and never flinched or wavered," said journalist Lawrence Shiller, whose interviews with Gilmore and other research formed the basis for Norman Mailer's powerful bestseller "The Executioner's Song."

"He didn't want to spend his life in prison and wanted to take the chance that there was a hereafter. He regretted what he had done, which had come out of an emotional relationship. He was venting his anger," Shiller said.
